description:
There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

metric_notes.sets_used: number of sets in the cover
metric_notes.mean_set_cost: average cost of a chosen set
metric_notes.mean_set_size: average size of a chosen set
metric_notes.covered_twice_pct: % of elements covered by two or more chosen sets
metric_notes.redundant_sets: chosen sets whose every element is also covered by another chosen set
metric_notes.shared_with_reference_pct: % of the optimal cover's sets that this cover also chose
metric_notes.one_new_picks: picks that covered exactly one new element
metric_notes.one_new_cost_pct: % of the total cost spent on picks that covered exactly one new element
metric_notes.late_cost_pct: % of the total cost spent on the picks made after 90% of the elements were covered

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `costs`: shape (k,), int: the cost of every candidate set, in index order.
- `new_cover`: shape (k,), int: how many still-uncovered elements each candidate contains (≥ 1).
- `sizes`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's full size (covered elements included).
- `covers`: shape (k, u), bool: `covers[i, e]` is True when candidate i contains uncovered element e; the u columns are all the still-uncovered elements, in index order (u = `covers.shape[1]`).
- `total`: int: the number of elements in the universe (it differs between instances: normalise by it).
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)), roughly in [-1, 1].
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Ratio of newly covered elements to full set size, minus covered-elsewhere redundancy: coverage novelty fraction."""
    k = len(costs)
    nc = np.asarray(new_cover, dtype=float)
    sz = np.asarray(sizes, dtype=float)
    # novelty: fraction of the set's elements that are new
    novelty = nc / np.maximum(sz, 1.0)
    # how concentrated the new elements are: redundancy signal via overlap with other candidates
    overlap = covers.astype(float) @ covers.astype(float).T  # (k,k) shared new-element counts
    np.fill_diagonal(overlap, 0.0)
    shared = overlap.sum(axis=1)
    # average competition per new element (normalised)
    comp = shared / np.maximum(nc * np.maximum(k - 1, 1), 1.0)
    val = novelty - comp
    return np.clip(val, -1.0, 1.0)
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Ratio of uncovered elements newly covered to the element's rarest availability among candidates."""
    k = len(costs)
    # For each uncovered element, how many candidates can cover it (scarcity)
    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # shape (u,)
    # Weight each covered element by its rarity: 1/avail
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0)
    # Sum rarity over the elements each candidate covers, normalised by cost
    weighted = covers.astype(float) @ rarity  # shape (k,)
    denom = np.maximum(costs, 1.0)
    score = weighted / denom
    # Normalise to roughly [-1, 1]
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(k)
    return score / scale
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
```
```python
    """Fraction of a candidate's uncovered elements that no other candidate also covers (exclusive gain)."""
    k, u = covers.shape
    # count how many candidates cover each uncovered element
    deg = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)          # shape (u,)
    # exclusivity weight per element: 1 if only this candidate covers it, else small
    excl = (deg <= 1.0).astype(float)
    inv = 1.0 / np.maximum(deg, 1.0)                 # rarity of each element
    gain_excl = covers @ excl                        # count exclusively-covered elements
    gain_rare = covers @ inv                         # rarity-weighted gain
    nc = np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0)
    # normalise: exclusive share and rarity density, both bounded
    excl_share = gain_excl / nc                      # in [0,1]
    rare_density = gain_rare / np.sqrt(nc)           # bounded-ish
    rare_density = np.tanh(rare_density)
    return np.column_stack([excl_share, rare_density])
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
```
```python
    """New-coverage fraction minus competition: shared new elements per new element, normalised."""
    nc = np.asarray(new_cover, dtype=float)
    sz = np.asarray(sizes, dtype=float)
    novelty = nc / np.maximum(sz, 1.0)
    # column sums of covers: how many candidates cover each uncovered element
    col_sums = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # (u,)
    # for each candidate, sum over its new elements of (col_sum - 1), i.e. competitors
    competitors = covers.astype(float) @ (col_sums - 1.0)  # (k,)
    comp = competitors / np.maximum(nc * np.maximum(len(costs) - 1, 1), 1.0)
    val = novelty - comp
    return np.clip(val, -1.0, 1.0)
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
```
    """Fraction of a candidate's still-uncovered elements that are 'rare' (appear in few candidates)."""
    # rarity weight of each uncovered element = 1 / (number of candidates covering it)
    freq = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)          # shape (u,)
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(freq, 1.0)             # rarer elements -> larger weight
    gained = covers.astype(float) @ rarity           # sum of rarity over newly covered elements
    # normalise by the max achievable rarity sum so it lands in [0, 1]
    denom = np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0) * (rarity.max() if rarity.size else 1.0)
    return np.nan_to_num(gained / np.maximum(denom, 1e-9), nan=0.0)

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Fraction of a candidate's uncovered elements that no other candidate also covers (exclusive gain)."""
    k, u = covers.shape
    # count how many candidates cover each uncovered element
    deg = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)          # shape (u,)
    # exclusivity weight per element: 1 if only this candidate covers it, else small
    excl = (deg <= 1.0).astype(float)
    inv = 1.0 / np.maximum(deg, 1.0)                 # rarity of each element
    gain_excl = covers @ excl                        # count exclusively-covered elements
    gain_rare = covers @ inv                         # rarity-weighted gain
    nc = np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0)
    # normalise: exclusive share and rarity density, both bounded
    excl_share = gain_excl / nc                      # in [0,1]
    rare_density = gain_rare / np.sqrt(nc)           # bounded-ish
    rare_density = np.tanh(rare_density)
    return np.column_stack([excl_share, rare_density])
feature.measures: Fraction of a candidate's uncovered elements that no other candidate also covers (exclusive gain).

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Ratio of uncovered elements newly covered to the element's rarest availability among candidates."""
    k = len(costs)
    # For each uncovered element, how many candidates can cover it (scarcity)
    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # shape (u,)
    # Weight each covered element by its rarity: 1/avail
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0)
    # Sum rarity over the elements each candidate covers, normalised by cost
    weighted = covers.astype(float) @ rarity  # shape (k,)
    denom = np.maximum(costs, 1.0)
    score = weighted / denom
    # Normalise to roughly [-1, 1]
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(k)
    return score / scale

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `costs`: shape (k,), int: the cost of every candidate set, in index order.
- `new_cover`: shape (k,), int: how many still-uncovered elements each candidate contains (≥ 1).
- `sizes`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's full size (covered elements included).
- `covers`: shape (k, u), bool: `covers[i, e]` is True when candidate i contains uncovered element e; the u columns are all the still-uncovered elements, in index order (u = `covers.shape[1]`).
- `total`: int: the number of elements in the universe (it differs between instances: normalise by it).
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)), roughly in [-1, 1].
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. ## How to work

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Rarity-weighted uncovered gain divided by a saturating cost denominator (cost + mean candidate cost), normalised."""

    val = val / (np.max(np.abs(val)) + 1e-12)
    return val
```

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Rarity-weighted gain per cost, with rarity scaled by element scarcity squared and by the element's residual cover depth."""
    k = len(costs)
    u = covers.shape[1]
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    c = covers.astype(float)
    avail = c.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # candidates covering each uncovered element
    # Rarity emphasising near-exclusive elements quadratically
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0) ** 2
    # Residual depth: fraction of the universe still uncovered, scales how much scarcity matters
    depth = u / max(total, 1)
    weighted = c @ rarity
    # Normalise per element count (so large sets don't just win by size)
    per_el = weighted / np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0)
    # Cost efficiency on top
    score = per_el * (1.0 + depth) / np.maximum(costs, 1.0)
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(k)
    return score / scale

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Rarity-weighted new coverage discounted by how many other candidates share the same elements, per unit of the candidate's remaining-cost burden."""
    cnt = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)          # availability of each uncovered element
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(cnt, 1.0)             # scarce elements matter more
    covered = covers.astype(float)                  # (k, u)
    # raw rarity gain
    gain = covered @ rarity
    # competition: for each candidate, average availability of the elements it covers
    avail_cov = covered @ cnt                        # sum of avail over covered elements
    ncov = np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0)
    comp = avail_cov / ncov                          # mean availability of its new elements
    # discount gain by competition intensity
    disc = gain / (1.0 + comp)
    # burden: cost per element of the candidate it would still "cover" (penalise big sets)
    burden = np.maximum(costs, 1.0) / np.maximum(sizes.astype(float), 1.0)
    score = disc / (1.0 + burden)
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(len(costs))
    return score / scale

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Exclusive gain weighted by cost-competitiveness: exclusive/rare elements covered per rival candidate, scaled by cheapness."""
    k, u = covers.shape
    deg = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)            # (u,) candidates covering each uncovered element
    # scarcity weight: strong for elements only a few candidates can take
    scarcity = 1.0 / (deg * deg)                       # (u,)
    # densely-covered elements contribute almost nothing, so only near-exclusive ones matter
    gain = covers.astype(float) @ scarcity            # (k,)
    nc = np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0)
    density = gain / nc                                # per-new-element scarcity density
    # thread of the parent's exclusivity, but relative to the field: how much of the element
    # space this candidate locks up compared to the best rival for the same elements
    excl = (deg <= 1.0).astype(float)
    locked = covers.astype(float) @ excl              # count of exclusively-held elements
    # cheapness of the candidate relative to the field (thread: parent cared about what you gain)
    c = np.maximum(costs.astype(float), 1e-9)
    cheap = (np.median(c) / c)                        # >1 when cheaper than typical
    cheap = np.tanh(np.log(np.maximum(cheap, 1e-9)))
    return np.column_stack([
        np.tanh(density),
        locked / np.maximum(gain, 1e-9) * cheap,      # exclusive share of scarcity, cheapness-weighted
    ])

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Fraction of universe still uncovered that this candidate would leave uncovered after choosing it, per cost efficiency."""
    # How many uncovered elements each candidate covers
    k = len(costs)
    u = covers.shape[1]
    # Elements covered by candidate i: covers[i, e]
    # Elements covered by at least one other candidate: for each element e, count of candidates covering it
    cnt = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # (u,)
    # For candidate i, elements it covers that are covered ONLY by it (exclusive) vs shared
    # After picking i, elements still uncovered = those not in i (u - new_cover) PLUS
    #   those in i but we consider them covered. So residual = u - new_cover[i].
    # But cost matters: residual / cost, negated so cheaper coverage of more wins.
    residual = (u - new_cover).astype(float) / max(u, 1)
    # Normalise by cost relative to mean cost among candidates
    mc = np.mean(costs) + 1e-9
    cost_rel = costs / mc
    # Lower residual per unit cost is better -> negative
    score = -residual / np.maximum(cost_rel, 1e-3)
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(k)
    return score / scale

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Ratio of uncovered elements newly covered to the element's rarest availability among candidates."""
    k = len(costs)
    # For each uncovered element, how many candidates can cover it (scarcity)
    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # shape (u,)
    # Weight each covered element by its rarity: 1/avail
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0)
    # Sum rarity over the elements each candidate covers, normalised by cost
    weighted = covers.astype(float) @ rarity  # shape (k,)
    denom = np.maximum(costs, 1.0)
    score = weighted / denom
    # Normalise to roughly [-1, 1]
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(k)
    return score / scale

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Rarity-weighted gain per cost, with rarity scaled by element scarcity squared and by the element's residual cover depth."""
    k = len(costs)
    u = covers.shape[1]
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    c = covers.astype(float)
    avail = c.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # candidates covering each uncovered element
    # Rarity emphasising near-exclusive elements quadratically
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0) ** 2
    # Residual depth: fraction of the universe still uncovered, scales how much scarcity matters
    depth = u / max(total, 1)
    weighted = c @ rarity
    # Normalise per element count (so large sets don't just win by size)
    per_el = weighted / np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0)
    # Cost efficiency on top
    score = per_el * (1.0 + depth) / np.maximum(costs, 1.0)
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(k)
    return score / scale

feature.name: exclusive_scarcity_per_cost
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Exclusive gain weighted by cost-competitiveness: exclusive/rare elements covered per rival candidate, scaled by cheapness."""
    k, u = covers.shape
    deg = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)            # (u,) candidates covering each uncovered element
    # scarcity weight: strong for elements only a few candidates can take
    scarcity = 1.0 / (deg * deg)                       # (u,)
    # densely-covered elements contribute almost nothing, so only near-exclusive ones matter
    gain = covers.astype(float) @ scarcity            # (k,)
    nc = np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0)
    density = gain / nc                                # per-new-element scarcity density
    # thread of the parent's exclusivity, but relative to the field: how much of the element
    # space this candidate locks up compared to the best rival for the same elements
    excl = (deg <= 1.0).astype(float)
    locked = covers.astype(float) @ excl              # count of exclusively-held elements
    # cheapness of the candidate relative to the field (thread: parent cared about what you gain)
    c = np.maximum(costs.astype(float), 1e-9)
    cheap = (np.median(c) / c)                        # >1 when cheaper than typical
    cheap = np.tanh(np.log(np.maximum(cheap, 1e-9)))
    return np.column_stack([
        np.tanh(density),
        locked / np.maximum(gain, 1e-9) * cheap,      # exclusive share of scarcity, cheapness-weighted
    ])

name: exclusive_scarcity_per_cost
feature.measures: Exclusive gain weighted by cost-competitiveness: exclusive/rare elements covered per rival candidate, scaled by cheapness.

feature.name: residual_per_cost
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Fraction of universe still uncovered that this candidate would leave uncovered after choosing it, per cost efficiency."""
    # How many uncovered elements each candidate covers
    k = len(costs)
    u = covers.shape[1]
    # Elements covered by candidate i: covers[i, e]
    # Elements covered by at least one other candidate: for each element e, count of candidates covering it
    cnt = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # (u,)
    # For candidate i, elements it covers that are covered ONLY by it (exclusive) vs shared
    # After picking i, elements still uncovered = those not in i (u - new_cover) PLUS
    #   those in i but we consider them covered. So residual = u - new_cover[i].
    # But cost matters: residual / cost, negated so cheaper coverage of more wins.
    residual = (u - new_cover).astype(float) / max(u, 1)
    # Normalise by cost relative to mean cost among candidates
    mc = np.mean(costs) + 1e-9
    cost_rel = costs / mc
    # Lower residual per unit cost is better -> negative
    score = -residual / np.maximum(cost_rel, 1e-3)
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(k)
    return score / scale

name: residual_per_cost
feature.measures: Fraction of universe still uncovered that this candidate would leave uncovered after choosing it, per cost efficiency.

feature.name: competition_discounted_rarity_per_burden
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Rarity-weighted new coverage discounted by how many other candidates share the same elements, per unit of the candidate's remaining-cost burden."""
    cnt = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)          # availability of each uncovered element
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(cnt, 1.0)             # scarce elements matter more
    covered = covers.astype(float)                  # (k, u)
    # raw rarity gain
    gain = covered @ rarity
    # competition: for each candidate, average availability of the elements it covers
    avail_cov = covered @ cnt                        # sum of avail over covered elements
    ncov = np.maximum(new_cover.astype(float), 1.0)
    comp = avail_cov / ncov                          # mean availability of its new elements
    # discount gain by competition intensity
    disc = gain / (1.0 + comp)
    # burden: cost per element of the candidate it would still "cover" (penalise big sets)
    burden = np.maximum(costs, 1.0) / np.maximum(sizes.astype(float), 1.0)
    score = disc / (1.0 + burden)
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(len(costs))
    return score / scale
feature.measures: Rarity-weighted new coverage discounted by how many other candidates share the same elements, per unit of the candidate's remaining-cost burden.

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Rarity-weighted new coverage times the candidate's purity (new_cover/sizes), per unit cost, max-abs normalised."""
    nc = new_cover.astype(float)
    sz = np.maximum(sizes.astype(float), 1.0)
    c = np.maximum(costs.astype(float), 1.0)
    purity = nc / sz
    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0)
    R = covers.astype(float) @ rarity
    val = (R * nc * purity) / c
    val = val / (np.max(np.abs(val)) + 1e-12)
    return val

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Negative cost of each candidate divided by the sum, over its newly covered elements, of the cheapest candidate cost covering each such element, normalised by max abs value."""
    costs_f = costs.astype(float)
    big = np.where(covers, costs_f[:, None], np.inf)

    val = -(costs_f / (alt + 1e-9))
    val = val / (np.max(np.abs(val)) + 1e-12)
    return val

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `costs`: shape (k,), int: the cost of every candidate set, in index order.
- `new_cover`: shape (k,), int: how many still-uncovered elements each candidate contains (≥ 1).
- `sizes`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's full size (covered elements included).
- `covers`: shape (k, u), bool: `covers[i, e]` is True when candidate i contains uncovered element e; the u columns are all the still-uncovered elements, in index order (u = `covers.shape[1]`).
- `total`: int: the number of elements in the universe (it differs between instances: normalise by it).
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)), roughly in [-1, 1].
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

```python
def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
```
```python
    """Rarity-weighted gain per cost, but rarity computed against the full candidate set coverage (including already-covered elements), so scarcity reflects global availability rather than only uncovered competition."""

    sizes_f = np.maximum(sizes.astype(float), 1.0)

    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
```

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Rarity-weighted uncovered gain per unit of (cost above the cheapest covering alternative), with the cost gap compressed by a log-saturating transform, normalised."""
    costs_f = costs.astype(float)
    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0)
    R = covers.astype(float) @ rarity
    R = R / (np.max(R) + 1e-12)
    # cheapest covering alternative per uncovered element (excluding self-effect via min)
    big = np.where(covers, costs_f[:, None], np.inf)
    min_c = big.min(axis=0)
    alt = covers.astype(float) @ min_c  # summed cheapest alternatives over new elements
    alt = np.maximum(alt, 1e-9)
    # cost gap relative to the alternatives: how much more this set costs than the cheapest way
    gap = (costs_f - alt) / alt
    # log-saturating compression: penalise expensive sets but flatten extremes
    denom = np.log1p(np.maximum(gap, 0.0)) + 1.0
    val = R / denom
    val = val / (np.max(np.abs(val)) + 1e-12)
    return val

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Marginal cost per element against the best alternative for each of the candidate's new elements, aggregated as a max regret."""
    costs_f = costs.astype(float)
    # Cost of each candidate per newly covered element
    per_elem = costs_f[:, None] / np.maximum(new_cover, 1)[:, None]  # (k,1) broadcast
    # For each uncovered element, the cheapest per-element cost among candidates covering it
    big = np.where(covers, per_elem, np.inf)  # (k,u)
    best = big.min(axis=0)  # (u,)
    # Regret of each candidate on each of its new elements: own per-elem cost minus best alternative
    regret = np.where(covers, per_elem - best[None, :], 0.0)  # (k,u)
    # Worst (max) regret over its new elements: how much worse than the best it is on its worst element
    worst = regret.max(axis=1)  # (k,)
    # Normalise: divide by (best + worst) or by max range -> use max per-element cost scale
    scale = np.max(np.where(covers, per_elem, 0.0)) + 1e-9
    val = -worst / scale
    return val

    """Rarity-weighted uncovered gain per unit of (cost above the cheapest covering alternative), with the cost gap compressed by a log-saturating transform, normalised."""
    costs_f = costs.astype(float)
    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0)
    R = covers.astype(float) @ rarity
    R = R / (np.max(R) + 1e-12)
    # cheapest covering alternative per uncovered element (excluding self-effect via min)
    big = np.where(covers, costs_f[:, None], np.inf)
    min_c = big.min(axis=0)
    alt = covers.astype(float) @ min_c  # summed cheapest alternatives over new elements
    alt = np.maximum(alt, 1e-9)
    # cost gap relative to the alternatives: how much more this set costs than the cheapest way
    gap = (costs_f - alt) / alt
    # log-saturating compression: penalise expensive sets but flatten extremes
    denom = np.log1p(np.maximum(gap, 0.0)) + 1.0
    val = R / denom
    val = val / (np.max(np.abs(val)) + 1e-12)
    return val

name: rarity_gain_saturating_cost
feature.measures: Rarity-weighted uncovered gain per unit of (cost above the cheapest covering alternative), with the cost gap compressed by a log-saturating transform, normalised.

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Marginal cost per element against the best alternative for each of the candidate's new elements, aggregated as a max regret."""
    costs_f = costs.astype(float)
    # Cost of each candidate per newly covered element
    per_elem = costs_f[:, None] / np.maximum(new_cover, 1)[:, None]  # (k,1) broadcast
    # For each uncovered element, the cheapest per-element cost among candidates covering it
    big = np.where(covers, per_elem, np.inf)  # (k,u)
    best = big.min(axis=0)  # (u,)
    # Regret of each candidate on each of its new elements: own per-elem cost minus best alternative
    regret = np.where(covers, per_elem - best[None, :], 0.0)  # (k,u)
    # Worst (max) regret over its new elements: how much worse than the best it is on its worst element
    worst = regret.max(axis=1)  # (k,)
    # Normalise: divide by (best + worst) or by max range -> use max per-element cost scale
    scale = np.max(np.where(covers, per_elem, 0.0)) + 1e-9
    val = -worst / scale
    return val

name: worst_element_cost_regret
feature.measures: Marginal cost per element against the best alternative for each of the candidate's new elements, aggregated as a max regret.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Rarity-weighted coverage where each element's weight is 1/(avail-1) when it has a second coverer, and a large finite weight when it is the last chance (avail=1) — cost-scaled by the candidate's share of covers of that element."""
    cnt = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # avail per uncovered element
    # weight: high for scarce elements, but distinguish 'last chance' (avail==1) strongly
    w = np.where(cnt <= 1.0, 4.0, 1.0 / np.maximum(cnt - 1.0, 1.0))
    # each candidate's contribution: how much of the element's cover burden it carries
    share = np.where(covers, 1.0 / np.maximum(cnt[None, :], 1.0), 0.0)
    v = share @ w
    v = v - 0.15 * (costs.astype(float) / (np.mean(costs.astype(float)) + 1e-9))
    scale = np.max(np.abs(v))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(len(costs))
    return v / scale
feature.measures: Rarity-weighted coverage where each element's weight is 1/(avail-1) when it has a second coverer, and a large finite weight when it is the last chance (avail=1) — cost-scaled by the candidate's share of covers of that element.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Reduced-cost surplus: (sum of per-element cheapest rates over newly covered elements - cost) / (sum + cost)."""
    eff = costs / np.maximum(new_cover, 1.0)
    M = np.where(covers, eff[:, None], np.inf)
    price = M.min(axis=0)
    fallback = eff.max() if len(eff) else 1.0
    price = np.where(np.isfinite(price), price, fallback)
    surplus = covers.astype(float) @ price
    values = (surplus - costs) / (surplus + costs + 1e-9)
    return values

idea.hypothesis: f004 prices a set only by its own rate; it never asks what the market charges for the elements it would take. Give every uncovered element a price = cheapest per-element rate among the candidates that cover it (min cost/new_cover). A candidate is worth taking exactly when its cost is below the sum of those prices (classic primal-dual reduced cost). Sets whose elements are cheaply obtainable elsewhere get negative surplus and lose, which is redundancy-aware efficiency rather than raw ratio.

import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Normalised new coverage minus normalised crowd (sum over newly covered elements of rivals sharing them)."""
    nc = new_cover.astype(float)

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `costs`: shape (k,), int: the cost of every candidate set, in index order.
- `new_cover`: shape (k,), int: how many still-uncovered elements each candidate contains (≥ 1).
- `sizes`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's full size (covered elements included).
- `covers`: shape (k, u), bool: `covers[i, e]` is True when candidate i contains uncovered element e; the u columns are all the still-uncovered elements, in index order (u = `covers.shape[1]`).
- `total`: int: the number of elements in the universe (it differs between instances: normalise by it).
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)), roughly in [-1, 1].
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

You are the **Researcher** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You are the deep loop: you work out *why* the current best candidate loses where it does, and you design experiments that find out. The Mutator, another agent, makes undirected variations; you cash in on what it stumbles on and on what your own experiments reveal.

## What you get

- the incumbent (the current best) and its parts: what each part actually does and how much the result relies on it;
- **diagnostics**: named metrics of the incumbent's results, next to a reference where one exists. This is where the mechanism shows;
- **sensitivity probes**: each part of the incumbent knocked out, weakened and amplified. A gain from amplifying means a direction is under-used; a loss from weakening means the incumbent relies on it;
- the **ledger** for the approaches you're assigned: what was tried, how it scored, and whether its prediction held;
- the **Mutator's recent finds**: things that scored well or nearly well without anyone knowing why. Explaining and sharpening a lucky find is often the best experiment available;
- your **assignments** from the Navigator: which approaches to work on, and how (explore a new one, exploit a promising one, probe a doubtful one).

## How to work

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.
2. **Design experiments of two kinds:**
   - `probe`: written to *learn*. Change one thing, or exaggerate one aspect, so the result tells you whether that aspect matters. Judged by whether its prediction held, not by its score.
   - `improve`: written to *win*.
3. **Don't repeat the ledger.** If an idea was tried, change it meaningfully or leave it. A disguised copy is detected and discarded. When the ledger shows a group of tried features that behave alike, that idea is spent: look at a different quantity altogether.
4. **Learn from what failed.** A prediction that didn't hold means the mechanism you believed is wrong or incomplete. Say what it taught you (`lesson`) before proposing the next experiment.
5. **Predict.** Every experiment names one metric from the diagnostics, where it should move (a family or scope), and the direction. The engine checks it.
6. **Be exact** in `change`: describe the candidate so precisely that it can be written without guessing.

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy: a weighted sum of **features** (measurements of a candidate in one decision). An optimiser fits the weights and their signs, so never choose numbers or signs: choose *what to measure*. # The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

```python
    """Rarity-weighted uncovered gain per unit of (cost above the cheapest covering alternative), with the cost gap compressed by a log-saturating transform, normalised."""

    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0)
    R = covers.astype(float) @ rarity
    R = R / (np.max(R) + 1e-12)
    # cheapest covering alternative per uncovered element (excluding self-effect via min)
    big = np.where(covers, costs_f[:, None], np.inf)
    min_c = big.min(axis=0)
    alt = covers.astype(float) @ min_c  # summed cheapest alternatives over new elements
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
```
    """Rarity-weighted new coverage per unit cost, but novelty-gated: rarity weight drops sharply for elements already heavily represented among candidates, and efficiency uses cost relative to the cheapest candidate covering the same elements."""

    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # (u,)

    weighted = covers.astype(float) @ rarity  # (k,)
    # cost relative to the cheapest alternative covering the same elements (per-element min, summed)
    big = np.where(covers, costs_f[:, None], np.inf)
    min_c = big.min(axis=0)  # (u,)
    alt = covers.astype(float) @ min_c  # sum of cheapest per new element

    blended = np.sqrt(np.maximum(costs_f, 1.0) * np.maximum(alt, 1.0))
    score = weighted / (blended + 1e-9)
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):

    return score / scale

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `costs`: shape (k,), int: the cost of every candidate set, in index order.
- `new_cover`: shape (k,), int: how many still-uncovered elements each candidate contains (≥ 1).
- `sizes`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's full size (covered elements included).
- `covers`: shape (k, u), bool: `covers[i, e]` is True when candidate i contains uncovered element e; the u columns are all the still-uncovered elements, in index order (u = `covers.shape[1]`).
- `total`: int: the number of elements in the universe (it differs between instances: normalise by it).
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)), roughly in [-1, 1].
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

- `covers`: shape (k, u), bool: `covers[i, e]` is True when candidate i contains uncovered element e; the u columns are all the still-uncovered elements, in index order (u = `covers.shape[1]`).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

```python
def _f004(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
    """Ratio of uncovered elements newly covered to the element's rarest availability among candidates."""
    k = len(costs)
    # For each uncovered element, how many candidates can cover it (scarcity)
    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # shape (u,)
    # Weight each covered element by its rarity: 1/avail
    rarity = 1.0 / np.maximum(avail, 1.0)
    # Sum rarity over the elements each candidate covers, normalised by cost
    weighted = covers.astype(float) @ rarity  # shape (k,)
    denom = np.maximum(costs, 1.0)
    score = weighted / denom
    # Normalise to roughly [-1, 1]
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):
        return np.zeros(k)
    return score / scale
```

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

- `costs`: shape (k,), int: the cost of every candidate set, in index order.
- `new_cover`: shape (k,), int: how many still-uncovered elements each candidate contains (≥ 1).
- `sizes`: shape (k,), int: each candidate's full size (covered elements included).
- `covers`: shape (k, u), bool: `covers[i, e]` is True when candidate i contains uncovered element e; the u columns are all the still-uncovered elements, in index order (u = `covers.shape[1]`).
- `total`: int: the number of elements in the universe (it differs between instances: normalise by it).
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)), roughly in [-1, 1].
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

```python
    avail = covers.sum(axis=0).astype(float)  # shape (u,)
    # Weight each covered element by its rarity: 1/avail

    denom = np.maximum(costs, 1.0)

    scale = np.max(np.abs(score))
    if scale <= 0 or not np.isfinite(scale):

    return score / scale
```

```python
def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
```

```python
    share = np.where(covers, 1.0 / np.maximum(avail[None, :], 1.0), 0.0)
```

- the **ledger** for the approaches you're assigned: what was tried, how it scored, and whether its prediction held;
- the **Mutator's recent finds**: things that scored well or nearly well without anyone knowing why. Explaining and sharpening a lucky find is often the best experiment available;
- your **assignments** from the Navigator: which approaches to work on, and how (explore a new one, exploit a promising one, probe a doubtful one).

## How to work

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.
2. **Design experiments of two kinds:**
   - `probe`: written to *learn*. Change one thing, or exaggerate one aspect, so the result tells you whether that aspect matters. Judged by whether its prediction held, not by its score.
   - `improve`: written to *win*.
3. **Don't repeat the ledger.** If an idea was tried, change it meaningfully or leave it. A disguised copy is detected and discarded. When the ledger shows a group of tried features that behave alike, that idea is spent: look at a different quantity altogether.
4. **Learn from what failed.** A prediction that didn't hold means the mechanism you believed is wrong or incomplete. Say what it taught you (`lesson`) before proposing the next experiment.
5. **Predict.** Every experiment names one metric from the diagnostics, where it should move (a family or scope), and the direction. The engine checks it.
6. **Be exact** in `change`: describe the candidate so precisely that it can be written without guessing.

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy: a weighted sum of **features** (measurements of a candidate in one decision). An optimiser fits the weights and their signs, so never choose numbers or signs: choose *what to measure*. The parts in the sensitivity probes are the kept features; amplifying one means multiplying its weight.

- `change` is the exact measurement, per candidate, in terms of the arguments, so a Coder can write it without guessing. Say what it is for the last or special candidates when that matters.
- **It must rank candidates differently.** A value that is the same for every candidate in a decision, or a monotone copy of a feature the policy already has, tells the optimiser nothing. Prefer comparisons between normalised quantities; use a hard threshold only when the condition is the idea.
- A `probe` feature changes one thing, or exaggerates one aspect (a sharper threshold, a stronger form, one condition only).

# The problem: Weighted set cover, built set by set

There is a universe of elements and a collection of sets, each a subset of the elements with a positive integer cost. A **cover** is a choice of sets whose union is the whole universe; the goal is the cheapest cover.

The cover is built one set at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next set to add; the **candidates** are all sets that contain at least one element not yet covered, in their original index order (so every set touching an uncovered element is a candidate). The chosen set is added for good, and the build stops when every element is covered. Nothing is removed afterwards, so a set made unnecessary by later choices still counts.

Four training families, 100-200 elements and 200-400 sets each, every element in at least two sets: `unicost` (every set costs 1; sets of 2 up to ~4% of the elements), `random_cost` (costs 1-100 independent of the set; sets up to ~8%), `size_cost` (cost about 10 × the set's size, ±40%; sets up to ~4%), `rare_elements` (random costs; a fifth of the elements lie in only one or two sets). Other families exist in testing. The **gap** of an instance is cost ÷ the optimal cost (from an integer program) − 1, in %.

```python
def feature(costs, new_cover, sizes, covers, total):
```
